inputs.original_text: This is exactly how they make an example of anyone who probes the machinery: focus everyone on the charges, then dismiss the group as purveyors of “false election claims.” Harry Wait requested ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without consent, and the jury convicted him of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge while acquitting him of another identity theft count. That split outcome doesn’t erase the bigger issue: he said he was demonstrating that the registration system could be exploited. The institutions benefit when people learn that testing the system can bring serious consequences—and when scrutiny itself gets treated as the threat.
inputs.modified_text: They want everyone focused on Harry Wait’s convictions instead of what his actions exposed. He requested ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without consent; the jury convicted him of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge, while acquitting him of another identity theft count. That split result is convenient: it lets institutions point to a verdict and dismiss the underlying question as “false election claims.” Wait said he was demonstrating that the registration system could be exploited. The real warning is that probing the machinery can be punished, while the people who benefit from keeping it unquestioned get to call the scrutiny the danger.
